newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD official welcomes greater BoE independence.
newsitem.headline: OECD official welcomes greater BoE independence.

text.p: Sweeping changes at the Bank of England announced on Tuesday are a step in the right direction towards independence and should be good news for the British economy, an official at the OECD economic think tank said.

The new British Labour government's decision to relinquish control over interest rates brings the Bank of England closer into line with its European counterparts and should boost its credibility, senior economist Hans Blommestein said.
And a parallel move to bring management of Britain's debt under Treasury control should free the 300-year-old central bank to do its main job of delivering stable prices to consumers.

"The general thrust is that the new government intends to give the central bank more independence to focus on its main task, meaning monetary policy with the principal aim of price stability," Blommestein, a senior economist at the OECD's financial affairs division, said in an interview.

British finance minister Gordon Brown, appointed last week after Labour's landslide election victory, stunned financial markets earlier on Tuesday by saying he would surrender "operational responsibility" over rates to the Bank of England.
He announced the decision shortly after raising interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point, a move he said would be his last interest rate decision under the previous system.
Blommestein said credible and predictable monetary policies usually led to lower rates and should be good for the economy.
"Experience shows this will be positive. There would be less volatility. More predictability of policy is good for the economy," he said.
The changes could also help the labour market by convincing unions inflation was to be kept under control, leading to lower demands for wage rises, he said.

The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development has long argued that a central bank model which puts price stability first, and is relatively free from intereference by the politicians, works most effectively.
Brown told a news conference a new nine-member committee at the Bank of England would set rates in future and pledged this would free it from "short-term political manipulation".

Disappointing some economists, however, Brown said the government would continue to set the inflation targets the Bank would have to follow in setting rates. And it would keep power to go back to fixing rates itself in "extreme" circumstances.
Blommestein said that did not necessarily mean the government would be tempted to wade in directly, but much would depend on how the checks and balances worked in practice.

A 1948 law in the Netherlands, for example, allows the Dutch finance minister to override the central bank, regarded as one of the most independent Europe. "But it has never been used because the procedure is extremely difficult," Blommestein said.
"What is more important is what kind of mandate a (central bank) governor has, how difficult it is to fire him in case of a dispute and how easy it is steer him with guidelines."
